scope_plain: Every City of Los Angeles voter. Not for people in other cities in LA County (Santa Monica, Culver City, West Hollywood, Burbank and so on). Los Angeles city offices are nonpartisan. If no one won a majority in the June 2 primary, the top two meet in this November runoff; most votes wins.
office_explainer: Runs city departments, proposes the $14.8 billion budget, picks the police and fire chiefs, can veto Council laws.
why_it_matters: The first incumbent LA mayor forced into a runoff since 2005. The next mayor decides whether to keep the Inside Safe homelessness program, how big LAPD should be, how the Palisades rebuild goes, and how the city handles the 2028 Olympics. The Council holds a lot of power too; this is a 'weak mayor' city.

candidates.name: Karen Ruth Bass
candidates.background: Mayor since 2022. Former member of Congress (2011 to 2022), Speaker of the California Assembly, physician assistant and founder of Community Coalition in South LA. Ballot designation: Mayor, City of Los Angeles. Finished first in June with 34.3%.

own_words.text: My top three priorities ... are ending street encampments ... strengthening public safety ... [and] elevating city services.
I will maintain focus on interim housing until the last street encampment is gone.
On the Trump administration: 'resistance with a purpose.' Says the city will protect residents from aggressive immigration enforcement while demanding federal aid it is owed.

Points to a 17.5% two-year drop in street homelessness, 40,000 housing units accelerated, the first rent stabilization update in 40 years, and the lowest homicide total since the 1960s. Opposes SB 79 (taller housing near transit). Backs Measure FD and signed the argument for Prop TE.

candidates.name: Nithya Raman
candidates.background: City Councilmember for District 4 (Silver Lake to Sherman Oaks) since 2020, urban planner, member of the Democratic Socialists of America. The first challenger to unseat an LA incumbent councilmember in nearly two decades. Ballot designation: Councilmember/Urban Planner. Finished second in June with 29.0%.

own_words.text: My top priority for improving quality of life is addressing housing and homelessness. ... Second, basic city services. ... Third, safer communities.
I promise to put real accountability at the center of Los Angeles' homelessness response so that every dollar spent is tied to measurable results.
As the author of L.A.'s Sanctuary City Ordinance, I have built the legal foundation that prohibits city resources ... from being used for federal immigration enforcement.

Says she passed the strongest tenant protections in city history, cut encampments in her district by 54%, and voted against the police contract and Convention Center deal that she says drove the city into a billion-dollar deficit. Wants to triple housing construction, fix 30,000 dark streetlights with a public dashboard, and expand the Council from 15 to 25 seats.

scope_plain: Every City of Los Angeles voter. Los Angeles city offices are nonpartisan. If no one won a majority in the June 2 primary, the top two meet in this November runoff; most votes wins. The incumbent, Hydee Feldstein Soto, finished third in June and is out.
office_explainer: The city's lawyer: writes ordinances, defends lawsuits, advises City Hall, and prosecutes misdemeanors (not felonies).
why_it_matters: An office of about 550 lawyers that decides which misdemeanors get charged, how hard the city fights or settles lawsuits (a huge budget cost), and how aggressively it enforces tenant, worker and consumer laws. It also leads the city's legal response to federal immigration enforcement.
incumbent: Hydee Feldstein Soto (eliminated in the primary)

candidates.name: John McKinney
candidates.background: Deputy District Attorney in the LA County DA's office, where he has worked in the Hardcore Gang Unit and Major Crimes Division and prosecuted the Nipsey Hussle murder case. Ran for DA in 2024. UCLA Law. Ballot designation: Deputy District Attorney. Second in June with 28.6%.

own_words.text: Would 'enforce 41.18,' the anti-camping law, using diversion rather than jail, and says the office can 'leverage' arrested homeless people into treatment.

Wants more prosecution of misdemeanor gun crimes, repeat quality-of-life offenders, retail theft, street racing and open-air drug markets; criticized the incumbent for breaking up specialized domestic violence and gangs-and-guns units.
Measures success by 'fewer lawsuits and lower liability costs,' with better training for city workers including police to avoid suits.
Says he will 'protect Angelenos against unconstitutional ICE raids and Trump administration overreach.'

candidates.name: Marissa Roy
candidates.background: Deputy Attorney General in the California Department of Justice (consumer protection). Previously outside counsel for LA County in its litigation against the first Trump administration, a staff attorney at the Public Rights Project, and a fellow in the City Attorney's office. Grew up in Monrovia. Ballot designation: Deputy Attorney General. First in June with 43.1%.

own_words.text: Wants to make the office 'the largest public interest law firm in Los Angeles,' devoting at least 20% of it to public rights work paid for by civil penalties and growing the public rights unit to 100 lawyers.
Would 'invest in successful but underscaled diversion programs' and enforce renter protections to prevent evictions.
Would 'immediately cut' outside counsel, using it only for conflicts or niche specialties, and invite the Controller to audit the city's lawsuit liability.
Says she would prosecute 'rogue ICE agents,' sue companies such as Palantir and private prison operators, and join multi-city suits against the federal administration.

'The city needs somebody who comes from the outside,' with business experience.

Would have voted against the current city budget for not funding enough law enforcement; opposes rent control, which he says 'creates slumlords' and 'drives prices up'; criticizes Inside Safe and says groups like the Salvation Army could do the job cheaper.

candidates.name: Barri Worth Girvan
candidates.background: Most recently community affairs director for County Supervisor Lindsey Horvath; earlier district director for Senate Majority Leader Bob Hertzberg, West Valley area director for Mayor Villaraigosa, and government affairs director for the Jewish Federation of Greater LA. Calls constituent services her 'bread and butter' and promises a 'strike team on steroids' to deliver what residents need.

Would use the 41.18 anti-camping law in sensitive areas, streamline housing permits so the state does not take over local control, grow LAPD from under 9,000 to 12,000 officers, and called ICE raids 'unconscionable.'

candidates.background: Co-director of the LA office of ACCE (Alliance of Californians for Community Empowerment), a tenant and economic justice organizing group. own_words.text: 'Safety for me means access to safe streets. It means good services, like the lights come on. Folks in this district don't feel served by the LAPD.'
'The quality of life for immigrants is tied to how well they organize at the workplace.'

candidates.name: Jose Ugarte

own_words.text: 'We need to take drastic measures on mental health and homelessness. Instead of putting all the money in housing, we need to allocate a lot more to mental health.'
Wants the city to create its own public health department for the first time since the early 1960s.
Supports mandatory treatment and job training for unhoused people, and wants to keep district rents affordable by encouraging lower-priced housing and discouraging luxury construction.

scope_plain: Every Los Angeles County voter, whether or not the Sheriff's Department patrols where you live (LAPD covers the City of LA). Nonpartisan. No one won a majority in June, so the top two are in a runoff.
office_explainer: Runs the nation's largest sheriff's department: county jails, courthouse security, and policing for 42 contract cities and unincorporated areas.
why_it_matters: A rematch. Luna beat Villanueva 61% to 39% in 2022. The department faces a federal Department of Justice investigation of Men's Central Jail (announced Sept 9, 2026), a state lawsuit over jail conditions, a recruiting shortage, deputy-gang allegations and a $4 billion budget. The Sheriff also helps secure the 2028 Olympics.

candidates.name: Robert G. Luna
candidates.background: Sheriff since 2022. Long Beach police chief for seven years before that; 36 years in law enforcement. Grew up in East LA; master's in public administration from Cal State Long Beach. First in June with 44.2%.

own_words.text: Says violent crime has fallen every year in areas the department patrols and homicides are down 25% since 2023; serious crime in LASD areas fell 12.5% in 2025.

Wants to replace Men's Central Jail with a treatment-focused Correctional Care Center but not close it without a replacement; asked the National Institute of Corrections to review the jails after deaths rose to 46 in 2025.
On civilian oversight: has 'no problem' with it and says disputes were over records County Counsel told him not to share. Keeps the Office of Constitutional Policing and the anti-deputy-gang policy.

candidates.name: Alex Villanueva
candidates.background: Sheriff from 2018 to 2022, after more than 30 years as a deputy rising to lieutenant. His term featured repeated clashes with the Board of Supervisors and investigations of critics. After leaving, the county placed him on a 'do not rehire' list over harassment and discrimination findings, which he denies. Second in June with 21.7%.

own_words.text: Says the department 'has just fallen apart' since he left and that he is running to restore it.
Would hire 2,000 deputies in two years, return every station to full staffing, and bring jail medical care back under the department by abolishing county Correctional Health Services.
On deputy gangs: 'the deputy gang narrative was a political campaign.' On oversight: 'Oversight is important, but it cannot be used as a weapon of political attacks.'

Fully fund Prop 36, widen CARE Court, find a way to provide involuntary treatment for people on the streets; no more high-speed rail money 'unless I see a realistic plan'; supports banning social media for children under 16.

Build near jobs and transit and fund rental subsidies to prevent homelessness; voted no on SB 79; wrote AB 648 on community college housing.
Lead author of AB 715 on antisemitism in schools and AB 1609 guaranteeing access to a real person for customer help; chairs the Select Committee on Retail Theft.

Allow multifamily housing in single-family zones, a vacancy tax on corporate owners, and repeal Costa-Hawkins and the Ellis Act.
'Abolish ICE'; opposes AB 715, saying it 'censors discussions around Palestine'; 'massively regulate AI' so it does not replace workers.

district: District 4 (Fullerton, Brea, Buena Park, La Habra, Placentia, Stanton, parts of Anaheim)
scope_plain: Voters in Orange County Supervisorial District 4, which includes all of Fullerton. Nonpartisan on the ballot, though the parties have each endorsed. No one won a majority in June, so the top two meet in a runoff.
office_explainer: One of five supervisors who set an $11 billion county budget: sheriff, jails, public health, CalOptima, roads in unincorporated areas.
why_it_matters: Open seat; Doug Chaffee is termed out. Democrats hold a 3-2 majority on the board, and Republicans are trying to flip this seat and District 5. June was close: Traut 33.3%, Shaw 31.3%, with Fullerton Mayor Fred Jung and La Habra's Rose Espinoza splitting the rest. Shaw lost this seat to Chaffee in 2018 by under a point.

candidates.name: Tim Shaw
candidates.background: President of the Orange County Board of Education (trustee since 2020); La Habra City Council 2008 to 2021 including mayor; former chair of the Orange County Transportation Authority. Government affairs director for the Pacific West Association of Realtors and adjunct political science professor at Rio Hondo College. Registered Republican. Ballot designation: Orange County Board of Education Trustee. Second in June with 31.3%.

own_words.text: 'We need to have a total homelessness solution. We need to help families with affordability, as well as encouraging business growth to create more jobs. We need fiscal responsibility and transparency from county government.'

On the budget: 'Fund the things that are necessary, the DA's office, the sheriff's (office), the firefighters ... and then you're gonna have to trim the sails.' Supports 'local control' on housing but says cities must comply with state mandates; backs density near transit.

On homelessness, wants mental health and addiction treatment first and a closer look at what spending is working; his late father was a county addiction counselor and he lost a brother to fentanyl. As an OC Board of Education trustee, backed charter schools and the 'Parents Bill of Rights.'

candidates.name: Connor Traut
candidates.background: Mayor of Buena Park (council since 2018); Centralia Elementary school board 2014 to 2018; board director of the Orange County Fire Authority. Attorney in his family's personal injury law firm; Chapman University and Chapman law. Fourth-generation OC resident, age 31. Registered Democrat. Ballot designation: Mayor/Business Owner. First in June with 33.3%.

own_words.text: Priorities: 'Address affordability to help working families stay in O.C. Reduce homelessness and focus on mental health and addiction. Combat crime and ensure fast emergency response times. Enhance our parks and repair our roads.'

'I support tenant protections, strong code enforcement against slumlords and rental assistance to keep people housed.' Would partner with cities on senior and workforce housing near jobs and transit and expand vouchers and ADUs.

Says he balanced Buena Park's budget every year, added ambulance units, and passed a Community Workforce Agreement requiring local hiring and union wages on city construction. Would hire more CalOptima eligibility workers so people stay enrolled under stricter federal rules.

district: District 3 (central Fullerton, including the Cal State Fullerton area)
scope_plain: Only Fullerton voters who live in the district. Fullerton elects its five councilmembers by district; Districts 3 and 5 are up this year. Nonpartisan. No primary; most votes wins. Four-year term, three-term limit. Check the district map at the city clerk's site; Kevin's brother may be in District 3 or 5, or in a district not up this year.
office_explainer: One of five Fullerton councilmembers who set the budget, hire the city manager and police chief, and decide land use.
why_it_matters: Fullerton closed a $3.8 million deficit this summer with cuts after the council rejected putting a sales tax on the ballot (so there is no Fullerton city measure this November). Police and fire take about 70% of the general fund. Roads, parks and downtown are the recurring issues. District 3 is an incumbent defending her seat against a businessman and nonprofit founder.

candidates.name: Shana Charles
candidates.background: Councilmember since 2022; Cal State Fullerton public health professor. Ballot designation: City of Fullerton Councilmember/Professor. Endorsed by the OC Democratic Party, Reps. Lou Correa and Derek Tran, Sen. Tom Umberg, Assemblymembers Sharon Quirk-Silva and Avelino Valencia, Supervisors Chaffee and Sarmiento, NUHW, UFCW and OCEA.

own_words.text: 'I led successful efforts to repave our streets and restore community events like First Night & 4th of July Fireworks.'
'I was the driving force behind Fullerton joining the lawsuit against U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement's racial profiling and other illegal practices.'

Says she secured funding for fire and police, helped create the Fiscal Sustainability Committee, holds weekly office hours, and will work to pave 100% of streets, restore parks and 'renew our commitment to a sustainably equitable future.'

candidates.name: Daniel Kim
candidates.background: Fullerton commissioner and businessman who describes himself as a corporate turnaround specialist. UCLA and Harvard. Co-founded the Dragon Kim Foundation, which funds youth service programs and scholarships, after his son was killed by a falling tree at Yosemite in 2015. Ballot designation: Fullerton Commissioner/Businessman. No campaign website found.

own_words.text: 'Professionally, I'm a turnaround specialist: when companies are failing, I move them back to profitability. As I learned about Fullerton's multimillion dollar budget deficit, I knew I needed to help.'

Would 'eliminate waste, make cuts, and increase revenue to fix Fullerton's budget crisis,' make sure police and firefighters 'have what they need,' and 'repair Fullerton's roads after years of neglect.'

district: District 5 (downtown Fullerton and south-central neighborhoods)
scope_plain: Only Fullerton voters who live in the district. Fullerton elects its five councilmembers by district; Districts 3 and 5 are up this year. Nonpartisan. No primary; most votes wins. Four-year term, three-term limit.
office_explainer: One of five Fullerton councilmembers who set the budget, hire the city manager and police chief, and decide land use.
why_it_matters: Fullerton closed a $3.8 million deficit this summer with cuts after the council rejected putting a sales tax on the ballot (so there is no Fullerton city measure this November). Police and fire take about 70% of the general fund. Roads, parks and downtown are the recurring issues. District 5 is open: Ahmad Zahra is not running again. Three candidates, so the winner may take it with well under half the vote.

candidates.name: Oscar Valadez
candidates.background: Chair of the Fullerton Planning Commission; also served on the Parks and Recreation and Transportation commissions. Owner of a family construction business, Stanford civil engineering graduate, born and raised in Fullerton. Ballot designation: Fullerton Commissioner/Businessowner.

own_words.text: 'Ensure Fullerton police and firefighters have the resources they need to protect our safety. Improve Fullerton roads. Enhance Fullerton parks and public spaces.'
'Balance and audit Fullerton's budget with more transparency. Build senior citizen and workforce housing in Fullerton. Protect the character of our neighborhoods.'
His site lists no named endorsers ('coming soon'); says he is backed by community leaders, educators, small business owners, labor and faith organizations.

candidates.name: Jozef Maldonado
candidates.background: Chemist (UC Davis, forensic science emphasis) appointed to the Fullerton Parks and Recreation Commission in 2024. Moved to Fullerton after the pandemic. Age 30. Endorsed by the OC Democratic Party, Councilmembers Zahra and Charles, and school trustee Vanesa Estrella. Ballot designation: Chemist.

own_words.text: 'Protect public safety funding to ensure strong response times. Expand funding for our Senior Mobility Program and increase access to community centers and services.'
'Invest in small business development and social spaces throughout downtown to streamline permitting and increase foot traffic for businesses along Harbor.'
Wants to revisit the downtown noise ordinance and the job cuts made to close the deficit, fix sidewalks and bike lanes, and has floated a tram to carry students downtown.

candidates.name: David Fischbein
candidates.background: Retired U.S. Navy veteran (aviation and maritime operations) now working in quality assurance, purchasing and government acquisition. B.S. in business administration. Age 54. Ballot designation: Quality Assurance Inspector. His campaign site's endorsements page is password protected; URL not confirmed.

own_words.text: 'Fullerton deserves a councilmember who will focus on responsible spending, safer streets, well-maintained infrastructure, responsive city services, and transparent government.'

Says his top concern is public safety and he would not support dismantling or defunding the police; wants long-term agreements with Cal State Fullerton and Fullerton College on student housing, transit and parking.

candidates.name: Amy Dudich

office: North Orange County Community College District Board of Trustees
district: Trustee Area 6 (parts of Fullerton and Anaheim)
scope_plain: Only voters in the trustee area. The North Orange County Community College District runs Fullerton College and Cypress College. Nonpartisan; most votes wins. Areas 1, 3 and 6 are up; Area 6 is the one that includes part of Fullerton. Check your sample ballot.
office_explainer: One of seven trustees overseeing Fullerton College, Cypress College and adult education, with a $574 million bond.

candidates.name: Jeffrey P. Brown
candidates.background: Incumbent trustee; registered professional engineer with master's degrees in engineering and public administration and 45 years of project management. Fullerton homeowner for 46 years. Ballot designation: NOCCCD Boardmember/Engineer.
